Yatrika: Forty-Two Million Trips

Pune, October 2026. Five weeks to Diwali, four days to a board pre-read, and a chief product officer who no longer trusts the number the whole company has been managed by.

1. The night before

At twenty past eleven on the night of Thursday 8 October 2026, Sneha Kulkarni was at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with three laptops open — her own, her daughter's, which had the only working HDMI cable, and a company machine locked to the finance dashboards. The rain had stopped. The board pre-read was due by 9 a.m. on Monday 12 October, and the slide she could not write was the first one.

Yatrika, where Sneha had been chief product officer for two years and eight months, sold intercity travel: private bus seats, a small intercity cab business, and, since 2023, an annual pass. The company's North Star metric, adopted in January 2024 and printed on the wall of the Pune office, was completed trips per year. FY26 had closed at 42.7 million completed trips, up 40 per cent, and the Series E term sheet on Aniruddha Joshi's desk was written against 45 million trips in FY27 with a milestone tranche at 52 million.

On 21 August, Kabir Sheikh, a staff data scientist in Toronto, had sent Sneha a note showing that 42.7 million was wrong. Not fraudulently wrong; wrong in the way that data quietly becomes wrong. A pipeline migration in February 2025 had begun counting each leg of a multi-leg booking as a separate completed trip. The corrected FY26 figure was 38.3 million. Between 21 August and tonight, Sneha had learned two further things that were each individually worse than the first, and she had not yet worked out what either of them meant.

2. How Yatrika got here, and the decision that still constrains it

Yatrika was founded in 2016 by Aniruddha Joshi and two classmates from COEP, on the observation that India's private bus market was large, fragmented and almost entirely offline outside a handful of aggregators. For its first five years it was a straightforward inventory business: sign operators, list seats, take a commission of 8 to 11 per cent, compete on selection and on refunds. By FY22 it had 6.1 million annual booking users and a reputation in Maharashtra and Karnataka for actually honouring cancellations, which redBus, AbhiBus and the state transport corporations' own booking channels did with varying grace.

Two decisions from that period constrain everything Sneha can propose tonight.

The first, in September 2022, was a three-year supply agreement with the Deccan Operators Consortium, a group of 240 private bus operators running Maharashtra and northern Karnataka routes. In exchange for preferential inventory and a 3 per cent commission advantage, Yatrika guaranteed a minimum offtake of 8.4 million seats a year on consortium routes, with a shortfall penalty of ₹29 crore. The agreement runs to March 2027. In FY26 Yatrika sold 8.9 million consortium seats, comfortably clear, but it did so partly by pushing a discounted short-route category that Meghna Iyer, the chief financial officer, now says loses money on every ticket.

The second, in April 2023, was Yatrika Pass: ₹1,199 a year for 15 per cent off every booking, free cancellation up to two hours before departure, and a dedicated support line. The Pass was designed by Sneha's predecessor as a frequency instrument. Within eighteen months 2.1 million were active, and the dashboards showed exactly what had been hoped for: Pass holders took 4.9 trips a year against 2.6 for everyone else. That single comparison, more than any other, set the company's strategy for three years. It is one of the two things Sneha learned in September.

3. The industry

Indian intercity travel is contested from four directions at once. redBus, part of the MakeMyTrip group, remains the reference brand in private bus booking; AbhiBus, under Ixigo, competes aggressively on price; Paytm and PhonePe sell bus tickets as a utility inside super-apps with distribution Yatrika cannot buy. Ola and Uber have both pushed intercity cab products. On the corridors that matter most to Yatrika's margins — Pune–Mumbai, Bengaluru–Mysuru, Nagpur–Hyderabad — Indian Railways is the real competitor, and the expansion of Vande Bharat services on several of these routes over the last two years has taken the most price-insensitive passengers off the buses. The state corporations, MSRTC and KSRTC, run their own apps and undercut private operators on the shortest routes.

Three regulatory facts shape the product. GST at 5 per cent on air-conditioned bus tickets sits inside the displayed fare and cannot be marketed away. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose consent requirements Yatrika implemented in a rush in late 2025, shrank the company's addressable notification base by 22 per cent, which removed the cheapest frequency lever the growth team had. And the Reserve Bank's rules on recurring e-mandates mean the Pass auto-renewal has to clear an additional factor of authentication that a meaningful share of users simply never complete — a mechanism whose consequences appear in Exhibit 3 and were, until June, invisible.

Yatrika's exposure is not only Indian. A white-label version of its booking engine runs for two Southeast Asian operators, managed by Wei-Ling Tan in Singapore, and Gulf Wasl Travel, a Dubai-based online travel agency, has a signed letter of intent for a GCC deployment worth ₹34 crore over three years, contingent on a January 2027 launch. Neil Varghese, who runs enterprise and white-label sales out of Jersey City, has been promising that launch since June.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence matters, because at each point the company believed something it no longer believes.

January 2024. Yatrika adopted completed trips per year as the North Star, in preference to gross booking value, on an argument Sneha herself made: fares are set by operators and fuel prices, so rupees measure the market, while trips measure how much travel Yatrika actually enables. The board accepted it. The metric was decomposed into three inputs that went on the same wall: annual booking users (breadth), trips per user per year (frequency), and average fare per trip (depth). Each had an owner — Rajat Bhandari in Bengaluru for breadth, Sneha for frequency, Farida Kagzi in Pune for the supply mix that determined depth.

Through FY25. Every input moved in the right direction, and the frequency number moved fastest. The Pass comparison was quoted in three successive board decks. Rajat's growth budget doubled.

February 2025. The analytics pipeline was migrated to a new event schema, a project run out of Bengaluru with Kabir's team in Toronto consuming the output. Multi-leg bookings — a Pune–Mumbai–Surat itinerary sold as one transaction — began emitting two completed-trip events. Nobody noticed, because the multi-leg share had been under 2 per cent when the schema was designed and had grown to 11 per cent by FY26 as the shuttle category fed connections.

March 2026. Rajat's team scaled a short-route shuttle category — Pune–Mumbai and Bengaluru–Mysuru at ₹99 to ₹149 introductory fares, standing inventory from consortium operators. Trips rose sharply. Average fare fell. Rajat's reading was that Yatrika had unlocked a commuter use case with structurally higher frequency; Meghna's reading was that Yatrika was buying trips at a loss to hit a number.

21 August 2026. Kabir's note: FY26 completed trips are 38.3 million, not 42.7 million. Gross booking value, which is reconciled against payment settlements rather than the event pipeline, is unaffected at ₹2,364 crore. The restatement therefore moves frequency down and average fare up.

4 September 2026. Kabir's second note: the Pass frequency effect is mostly selection. A matched comparison, on the subset of users for whom a pre-purchase travel history exists, puts the incremental effect at 0.4 trips a year, not the 2.3 the dashboards had shown.

19 September 2026. Finance closed a review of Pass renewals. The renewal rate reported to the board for FY26 — 68 per cent — had been computed over Pass holders whose e-mandate was still active at expiry. Computed over all expiring Passes, it is 41 per cent.

2 October 2026. Neil escalated the Gulf Wasl timeline. Fourteen engineers for five months, starting immediately, or the January launch is gone and, Neil believes, so is the contract. The same fourteen engineers are the platform team holding the Diwali capacity work.

5. The people

Sneha Kulkarni, Chief Product Officer, Pune. Position: the company cannot go into a Series E on a number it has just restated, and the decomposition beneath the number needs rebuilding before the metric is defended. Incentive: she chose the North Star and owns frequency, the input most damaged by the restatement. Not saying: she believed the Pass frequency result for two years without asking whether it was causal, and her own 2024 roadmap was built on it.

Aniruddha Joshi, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Position: the restatement is an accounting matter, the trajectory is unchanged, and the board should be told about the correction in the appendix. Incentive: the Series E term sheet expires on 30 November and is priced on trips. Not saying: he has told two existing investors that FY27 will clear 50 million trips.

Meghna Iyer, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. Position: trips is the wrong North Star; contribution margin per booking is the only number that has ever predicted Yatrika's cash position, and the shuttle category should be shut. Incentive: she is accountable for a ₹340-crore cash balance and 19 months of runway. Not saying: her own margin model allocates the consortium shortfall penalty across all consortium seats, which is what makes the shuttle look negative; on an incremental basis, below the 8.4-million guarantee, the allocation is arguable.

Rajat Bhandari, VP Growth, Bengaluru. Position: the shuttle category is the only place in the business where a user travels more than once a month, and killing it kills the company's only habit. Incentive: his team's objectives are written in booking users and trips. Not saying: 31 per cent of shuttle trips in the last quarter came from users acquired by a ₹49 cashback funded from the brand budget, not the growth budget, so his cost per trip understates the true cost.

Farida Kagzi, Head of Supply and Operator Partnerships, Pune. Position: whatever is decided, the consortium's 8.4 million seats must be sold by March or Yatrika pays ₹29 crore and loses its inventory advantage at renewal. Incentive: her relationships with 240 operators, several of whom have been approached by AbhiBus. Not saying: two of the largest consortium members have already told her they intend to renegotiate commission at renewal regardless.

Kabir Sheikh, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the company should restate two years of input metrics publicly to its board and stop reporting any ratio it cannot compute within a cohort. Incentive: professional credibility, and a promotion case that rests on the rigour of this analysis. Not saying: the Pass dashboard that produced the naive 4.9-versus-2.6 comparison was built by his own team in 2023, and he has not corrected it for eighteen months.

Johanna Reiss, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the app has been optimised for rebooking a route the user has already taken, which is why frequency looks like the company's strength and discovery of new routes has atrophied; the home screen is a frequency machine that has quietly capped breadth. Incentive: she has been arguing for a discovery redesign for a year and this is her opening. Not saying: her redesign would slow the booking flow by two steps, and the Bengaluru team has measured that conversion falls 4 per cent for each added step.

Wei-Ling Tan, Head of Customer Success, International, Singapore. Position: the white-label business is the only part of Yatrika with positive unit economics from day one and it is being starved. Incentive: her retention targets are on white-label clients. Not saying: the Southeast Asian operators have asked for a contractual uptime commitment during Diwali that Yatrika's platform has never met.

Neil Varghese, Head of Enterprise Sales, Jersey City. Position: Gulf Wasl signs in October or not at all. Incentive: the contract is 40 per cent of his annual quota. Not saying: Gulf Wasl's own procurement has told him informally that a March launch would be acceptable with a price concession.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. The North Star as reported to the board, FY24 to FY26 (from the metrics wall, as at July 2026)

Exhibits 1 and 2 cannot both be the basis of a plan, and the difference is not merely 4.4 million trips. 7. Voices

Aniruddha Joshi, in the executive meeting, 24 September"Nobody is disputing Kabir's arithmetic. I am disputing what we do with it four weeks before a term sheet. The business did what the business did. The counter was wrong. Put it in the appendix, say we have fixed the pipeline, and let us talk about Diwali."
Meghna Iyer, email to Sneha and Aniruddha, 25 September, 11.52 p.m."I have watched us manage to trips for two and a half years and the only thing that has grown faster than trips is the cost of a trip. ₹71 to ₹53 in contribution, Sneha. If the Series E is priced on a number we have just restated, we are going to spend FY28 explaining ourselves. Price it on gross booking value and margin and we will get a lower valuation and a company that is still here."
Rajat Bhandari, on the growth Slack channel, 6 October"Genuine question. Shuttle is 6.1 m trips and the only cohort in Yatrika that books twice a month. If we shut it, our frequency number goes back to something a railway timetable could have predicted. Everyone in this thread wants a habit business. This is the only habit we have got."
Johanna Reiss, on the same thread, 6 October"It is a habit on one route. Look at routes-per-user: 1.31 in FY24, 1.18 in FY26. We are getting better and better at selling the same journey to the same person and worse at everything else. That is why breadth has slowed, and no amount of arguing about frequency will fix it."
Kabir Sheikh, note to Sneha, 4 September"I want to be careful. The matched estimate is the best I can do and it is not good. If you need one sentence for the board it is this: we do not know whether the Pass creates travel, and the dashboard that said it does was built by my team and should have been caught in 2024."
Farida Kagzi, WhatsApp to Sneha, 7 October, 7.14 a.m."Deccan meeting done. They are asking for the Diwali allocation by Monday. If shuttle stops, my consortium number for the year is 6.9 m against 8.4 m. Please do not decide this without me in the room."
Neil Varghese, to Aniruddha, 2 October"Dubai is not going to wait while we rebuild a dashboard. This is 40 per cent of my number and the only deal in the pipeline with a signature on a letter of intent."

8. The options as Sneha sees them

Late on Thursday night, Sneha had written four options on the back of a printout. She was aware, in the way one is aware of something at half past eleven, that the list might be the wrong list.

One: hold the line. Keep completed trips as the North Star, disclose the restatement in the appendix as Aniruddha wants, protect Diwali with the full platform team, and go into the Series E on the restated 38.3 million with a revised FY27 target of 45 million. The three inputs stay as they are and the discussion about what they mean waits until January.

Two: change the number. Recommend that the board replace completed trips with something that has margin in it — contribution-positive trips, or gross booking value net of Pass discount — and accept that the growth story is reset in the middle of a raise. Meghna would support it; Rajat's targets would all have to be rewritten five weeks before peak.

Three: keep the number, rebuild the decomposition. Leave trips as the North Star but change the inputs: breadth measured as travellers who took at least two trips in the year, frequency measured within cohort rather than in aggregate, depth measured as contribution per trip rather than fare. Spend 26 engineer-months on the pipeline rebuild, which comes out of either Diwali or Dubai.

Four: fix the Pass. Reprice or retire the Pass, on the ground that its frequency claim is unproven and its discount is what has been eating depth. This is the cleanest financial act available and the one with the most immediate customer consequence, five weeks before the biggest travel fortnight of the year.

What the list does not contain is worth noticing. It contains no option in which the frequency of intercity bus travel is simply a property of Indian life — a category in which a household travels two or three times a year for a wedding, a festival and an examination, and no product can change that much — which would make the entire frequency programme a three-year argument with the calendar. It contains no option built on the one factor nobody has proposed to move: what Yatrika earns per trip through things it actually controls, such as seat selection, cancellation cover, terminal transfers and baggage, which currently contribute ₹11 of the ₹53. And it treats the choice as a choice about a metric, when Exhibit 6 says the binding constraint for the next five months is fourteen engineers, and Farida's message says the binding constraint for the next five days is a seat allocation she needs by Monday.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board pre-read is due at 9 a.m. on Monday 12 October; the board meets on Thursday 15 October. The Series E term sheet, at a pre-money valuation of ₹4,100 crore, expires on 30 November and carries a milestone tranche of ₹180 crore contingent on 52 million FY27 trips on the metric definition in force at signing — a clause Meghna has flagged twice and which nobody has yet re-read in the light of Exhibit 2. Cash is ₹340 crore, giving 19 months at the current burn of ₹18 crore a month, and a hiring freeze is in force. The Deccan Operators Consortium agreement runs to 31 March 2027 with an 8.4-million-seat minimum and a ₹29-crore shortfall penalty; Farida's projection without the shuttle category is 6.9 million. The Gulf Wasl signature window closes on 31 October. Fourteen platform engineers have 84 engineer-months to give and four claims totalling 178 on the table. Diwali falls on 8 November, and bookings for the festive fortnight open on 18 October.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Write Yatrika's North Star as an identity of its three inputs for FY24 to FY26 using Exhibit 1, then again using Exhibit 2. What changes about the story the company has been telling itself, and which of the two exhibits would you put in front of the board?

2. Exhibit 3 offers two estimates of the Pass's frequency effect that differ by a factor of nearly six. What would you need to believe for each to be the better estimate, and what would you have done differently in 2023 to avoid being in this position?

3. Exhibit 4's footnote undermines the exhibit's own conclusion in two distinct ways. Rework the shuttle row under each correction. Does the category now belong in the business, and on what basis would you decide?

4. Johanna's routes-per-user figure — 1.31 falling to 1.18 — is not in any exhibit. Where would it sit in a decomposition of completed trips, and what does its absence from the metrics wall suggest about how the inputs were chosen in January 2024?

5. Exhibits 5 and 6 describe constraints of very different kinds. If the festive peak, the Dubai contract, the pipeline rebuild and the discovery redesign cannot all be funded, what sequence would you choose, and which of the four stakeholders would you knowingly disappoint?

6. What should Sneha do on Monday morning — and what, precisely, should she say to the board on Thursday about a number the company has managed by for two and a half years, a milestone clause written against it, and the possibility that the frequency on which the strategy rests was never there?

11. Baner, half past one

At half past one Sneha closed the finance laptop and left the other two open. On one screen was Kabir's matched-cohort notebook, its confidence interval running from almost nothing to something that mattered. On the other was the pre-read template, with the title of the first slide typed and deleted four times. Outside, the last of the water was moving down the lane towards the nullah, and a bus was idling somewhere on the Mumbai road with its horn going.

She thought about Farida needing a seat allocation by Monday, and about the clause in the term sheet that said "on the metric definition in force at signing", and about the fact that the honest version of the first slide and the fundable version of the first slide were not the same slide. She had three days. She did not yet know which number she was going to defend.

Breadth × Depth × Frequency

An identity, not a theory: how many, how much, how often — and why the arithmetic is the easy part.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On Tuesday, 8 September 2026, Shalini Bhide, chief product officer of Ushas Learning Systems in Bengaluru, took a decision she had postponed a month. Ushas Abhyaas, the company's AI-tutored app for engineering and medical entrance aspirants, had 42 lakh registered learners, two-thirds outside the eight largest cities. Its North Star — solved-and-reviewed questions per registered learner per week — had climbed from 3.10 to 4.97 over twelve months, then sat between 4.90 and 5.00 for nine consecutive weeks. Bhide had ₹18 crore of budget to March 2027 and three proposals: Kannada and Bengali question banks, from a content lead in Kolkata; a longer "explain my mistake" flow from Rohit Nadgouda's modelling group in Hyderabad; and a streak-and-reminder system already piloted. One carried a variable cost the others did not — each generated explanation cost about ₹0.42 in inference — and the flat North Star said nothing about which to fund.

Two days later in Chennai, Kabir Sheth of Unnat Systems faced the mirror image. Unnat Floor, his warehouse-and-despatch execution software, ran in 214 mid-market manufacturers and logistics firms across 18,400 licensed seats carrying ₹96 crore of recurring revenue. Sixty-one contracts worth ₹34 crore fell due in the March quarter, and the pattern was clear: accounts confirming more than 180 despatch lines per licensed seat per week renewed at 94 per cent; accounts below 120 renewed at 58. The blended figure was 251.8. Meenakshi Rao, running customer success from Jamshedpur, insisted half the seats belonged to supervisors who touched the system once a week. The platform team insisted the product did too little per shift.

Neither lacked data. Both lacked a way of splitting one rate into terms different teams could own and argue about in a common currency. The split is trivial arithmetic; the definitional choices beneath it are not; and almost every expensive mistake made with it comes from treating an accounting identity as a causal model.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Let P be a base population, A those members who perform a qualifying behaviour within a chosen window, O the number of occurrences, V the value they produce. The North Star rate factors exactly:

V / P  =  (A / P)  ×  (O / A)  ×  (V / O)
            = breadth × frequency × depth

The adjacent denominators cancel: that is the whole trick and the whole warning. The equation is true by construction for any V, O, A and P you define, so it can never be falsified and can never be evidence. What it buys is a partition — three mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive terms, each ownable by a different team.

Figure 1. A telescoping product across one chain of denominators. A factorisation that does not telescope is not this framework; it is a model, and must be defended as one.

The lineage predates software. In 1912 Donaldson Brown at DuPont factored return on equity into margin × asset turnover × leverage, establishing the habit of governing a company through an identity whose terms map onto departments. Andrew Ehrenberg's repeat-buying work from 1959 onwards built the same split empirically — penetration, purchase frequency, weight of purchase — and found that brands of different sizes differ far more in penetration than in loyalty. The software version crystallised in consumer growth teams around 2009 to 2013, where "raise engagement" proved impossible to staff and "raise how many, how much, how often" proved straightforward. The problem it solves is organisational before analytical: an aggregate cannot be delegated; a decomposition can.

Four positions are held by serious people. The identity school would sign that any rate North Star should be factored into three to five ownable terms, each with an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs; it would not sign that those terms are independent levers. The penetration-first school, after Ehrenberg and Byron Sharp, would sign that in repeat-purchase categories most of the gap between a large and a small competitor is breadth, and that frequency follows penetration rather than leading it; it would not sign that a team should attack whichever factor looks weakest. The loop school would sign that where habit or network dynamics exist, frequency is upstream of breadth, because repeat use generates the content, referrals and rankings that bring the next user. The individual-level school, after Fader and Hardie, would sign that the three factors summarise a heterogeneous distribution and that a product of averages conceals the covariance deciding outcomes; it would not sign that the decomposition is useless. Most practitioners hold a blurred mixture of all four, which is why metric arguments take so long.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice begins with three definitional choices amateurs skip, each of which silently determines the answer. The qualifying behaviour: for Ushas, a learner who solved and reviewed a question, not one who opened the app; for Unnat, a seat that confirmed a despatch line. The window: a week for both. The base: Ushas divides by all registered learners ever, including lakhs who signed up before an exam and vanished; Unnat divides by licensed seats, a quantity set by its customers' procurement teams.

The first serious analysis is attribution of change, where teams introduce an error of about a sixth. Over the year to September 2026, Ushas breadth rose from 0.108 to 0.135 (+25.0 per cent), frequency from 2.90 to 3.20 (+10.3), depth from 9.9 to 11.5 (+16.2). The North Star rose 60.3 per cent, but the three gains sum to 51.5. The missing 8.8 points are interaction, because (1+β)(1+φ)(1+δ) exceeds 1+β+φ+δ whenever more than one factor moves. A team reporting "breadth contributed 25 points, frequency 10, depth 16" has lost a seventh of its own growth and will meet it next quarter as an unexplained residual. The remedies are the exact multiplicative form or logarithms: ln(4.97/3.10) = 0.4715 splits without remainder into 0.2231, 0.0983 and 0.1501. Log contributions add; percentages do not.

The third and most consequential piece is allocation. Because the factors multiply, one per cent of relative gain in any of them is worth the same one per cent in the North Star. The step usually left implicit is what follows: none of those numbers is a partial derivative, because the factors are not orthogonal in practice even though they are in algebra. Sheth's team learned this expensively. Their seat-activation plan promised breadth from 0.610 to 0.700, which the arithmetic said would carry the North Star to 289.0. But accounts already above 0.75 breadth showed depth of 82 lines per shift, not 96, because the marginal activated seat belongs to a supervisor, not a picker. With breadth 0.700 and depth 88 the result is 264.9 — a gain of 5.2 per cent rather than 14.8. Two-thirds of the promised benefit was a mix effect that would have surfaced as a mysterious depth decline and been blamed on the product.

4. When the decomposition applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions state as testable claims. One: the North Star is a rate over a population, not a stock. Both protagonists pass. Two: the behaviour repeats within the window, in practice frequency above about 1.2; at 1.0 the factor is a constant and the framework degenerates to breadth × depth. Ushas at 3.2 and Unnat at 4.3 pass. Three: occurrences are discrete, countable and value-bearing. An occurrence at Ushas is a session with a review step; counting app opens would fill the depth denominator with noise. Four: the base is stable relative to the window. Ushas partly fails — registrations spike each January and June around exam cycles, so breadth falls mechanically with no behaviour change. Unnat passes, since seat counts move only at contract events. Five: the factors are separately ownable. Ushas passes; Unnat does not, its breadth being set partly by customers' procurement teams buying seat blocks.

It actively misleads in four situations. In structurally low-frequency categories — term insurance, home loans, wedding services, capital purchases — frequency is bounded near one by the nature of the good, and a team told to move it will burn budget annoying customers. Where a few accounts carry most value, average depth describes nobody. Where more usage means the product is failing — fraud alerts, support tickets, exception queues — every factor points the wrong way. And where user and payer differ, the base is a commercial artefact and breadth measures how aggressively seats were sold.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies. The identity does not compose. With two products the company rate is (V₁+V₂)/P, and no multiplication of the per-product decompositions reaches it; value must be summed first, divided once. You must then decide whether company breadth means "used any product" or the average of per-product breadths. The two differ by the overlap, which is what a platform bet is actually about.

Two-sided marketplaces. Viraam Stays, a homestay marketplace in Goa and Himachal Pradesh, ran the decomposition on travellers and concluded it needed higher booking frequency. Run on supply, it told a different story: of 14,200 listed properties only 46 per cent had any availability loaded. A marketplace has two decompositions plus a liquidity term belonging to neither, and the binding constraint is rarely on the side easier to instrument.

Regulated products. In Indian financial services the frequency lever is partly a legal object. Commercial messaging runs through TRAI's distributed-ledger registry with pre-registered headers and templates; consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is purpose-bound; conduct rules limit how often an intermediary may approach a customer. The identity still holds; one of its terms is simply not a decision variable.

Hardware plus software. Vamika Devices, a Coimbatore maker of connected water-purification units, faced a denominator with three readings: units shipped, sold through, or activated in the app. Breadth over shipped units fell every time distribution improved, because stock in a distributor's godown joined the denominator months before the numerator. And frequency was set by physics — a filter changes every ninety days — leaving depth the only real dial.

AI-native products. Ushas shows three problems at once. Depth carries marginal cost, so deeper sessions worsen unit economics before they improve them. Session boundaries dissolve when an agent works in the background, making frequency arbitrary. And a better tutor should reduce frequency: a learner who masters a topic in two sessions instead of five is a success the North Star records as decline. Quality-adjusted depth is the right instinct, though harder to instrument and easier to game.

At the organisational seams. Breadth lives in marketing, frequency in lifecycle, depth in monetisation; the identity makes their proposals comparable while leaving their externalities invisible, since each team's lever moves the other two. What mature companies say they do is give one factor to each team with a quarterly target. What they actually do, once burned, is appoint a referee owning the definitions and the weekly reconstruction, set each target with the other two as guardrails, and restate the base once a year as a documented change.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

A relative point is worth the same anywhere, so the weakest factor is not automatically the right one. The competent practitioner sees breadth of 0.135 and sees a problem; the expert asks what a point costs in each factor and how much room is left. The tell is a plan justified by a metric's level rather than the price of moving it; levels reflect the category, not the team.

Breadth gains dilute depth and frequency mechanically. Every activation push adds people at the light end of the distribution, so blended depth and frequency fall though nobody's behaviour changed. The tell is depth declining in exactly the weeks marketing spend rose while cohort depth holds flat. Experts split change into within-cohort and between-cohort parts before reacting.

The window decides how much signal sits in frequency. Shorten it and frequency compresses toward one while variance migrates into breadth; lengthen it and the reverse. The tell is a frequency series whose standard deviation is under five per cent of its mean: a saturated factor, not a stable one, and the team is tracking a constant while believing it tracks behaviour.

The identity is exact, therefore it is never evidence. "The decomposition shows frequency caused the decline" mistakes an accounting statement for a causal one. Decomposition localises a change; it cannot attribute it, since a frequency fall may follow a depth change two months earlier. The tell is "because" following a factor name with no experiment in between.

The base is a choice that behaves like a performance. Ushas breadth of 0.135 over all-time registrations becomes 0.31 over learners registered in the last ninety days. Neither is wrong; only one can be used consistently. The tell is a step change in breadth with no matching step in absolute active users — the signature of a redefinition, often done innocently in a data migration.

The unit chosen for depth smuggles in the strategy. Depth in rupees, items, minutes or "value-creating actions" yields four pictures of one behaviour and four roadmaps. Unnat measures despatch lines rather than rupees because lines track the customer's labour saving, which is what renewal turns on. The tell is a depth unit nobody can trace to a customer outcome.

Averages of ratios and ratios of averages differ by the covariance, and the covariance is the interesting part. Table 2's fourteen per cent gap states that heavy learners are also deep learners. A rising Cov(f,d) means value is concentrating in a committed core — excellent for monetisation, dangerous for breadth. The tell is a checksum that misses and gets rounded away.

Factors trade against each other, invisibly, for about a month. A discount that raises frequency shrinks basket size; a longer explanation that raises depth cuts how many sessions fit in a week. The tell is a launch where the targeted factor moves exactly as forecast and the North Star moves half as much.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

The arithmetic is identical everywhere; most claimed differences between product types are differences in which factor has slack. In consumer products the base is behavioural and all three factors are genuine dials. In B2B and enterprise the base is contractual: breadth measures seat activation and is co-owned with sales, frequency is set by the customer's operating rhythm — shifts, month-end closes, sprint cycles — and is near-immovable, and depth is where product work pays. In marketplaces a single decomposition is a category error: you need one per side plus a liquidity measure. In hardware at least one factor is set by physics or channel inventory. In AI products depth carries marginal cost and better quality can reduce frequency, so the metric must be quality-adjusted or it punishes the product for working.

Stage changes practice more than product type does. Before product-market fit the factors are dominated by sampling noise, and the honest instruction is to count consistently and look at individual users rather than ratios. At early scale the value is definitional discipline — writing down what active means so next year's comparison is real. At scale the factors carry owners, cadences and budgets, and the cost-per-point table becomes the planning artefact. Later the interesting quantity migrates upward, to cross-product breadth.

8. Three worked examples

Vagmi Audio, Pune, November 2025 to March 2026. The regional-language audio-story app measured listening hours per registered user per month: base 96 lakh, breadth 0.21, frequency 9.4 sessions, depth 0.38 hours per session, giving 0.75 hours. The content team's instinct was more titles, a ₹3.2 crore breadth play. The factor series said otherwise: breadth and frequency were flat across five months while depth slid from 0.47 to 0.38, coinciding precisely with heavier mid-roll advertising. Capping ad load cost ₹40 lakh and restored depth to 0.47, taking the North Star to 0.928 hours, up twenty-four per cent. The decomposition did not prove the ads were the cause; it narrowed a five-month mystery to a two-week investigation.

Viraam Stays, quarter ended June 2026. Traveller-side figures were breadth 0.09, frequency 1.3 bookings, depth ₹11,400, giving ₹1,334 of gross bookings per registered traveller. The demand team proposed a ₹5 crore re-engagement campaign against frequency. The supply-side decomposition — 46 per cent of 14,200 properties with any availability, 6.1 booked nights each, ₹3,150 a night — pointed at calendar coverage instead. A ₹1.4 crore integration syncing host calendars with the two channel managers most Indian homestay owners already used lifted host breadth to 61 per cent, and traveller frequency rose to 1.6 with no demand-side spend, carrying the North Star to ₹1,642. Frequency was the symptom; supply breadth was the disease.

Umeed Insurance Services, Mumbai, 2025 — the failure. Umeed, a motor and term-life distributor, imported the consumer playbook wholesale, declared policies in force per registered customer its North Star and stood up a frequency squad. Purchase frequency in its categories ran at 1.08 a year, a fact about insurance rather than about Umeed. The squad spent ₹4.7 crore of a ₹6 crore budget over three quarters on cross-sell messaging, prompts and rewards; frequency moved to 1.11. Complaints against the company's registered message headers rose sharply, uninstalls ran at 2.3 times the prior year, and the metric that actually drove economics — thirteenth-month persistency, stuck at 71 per cent — belonged to nobody, because it was not a term in the identity anyone had written down. The recovery replaced the decomposition with a cohort survival model: premium per acquired customer as first-year premium multiplied by year-on-year persistency, by channel. Persistency reached 79 per cent, worth roughly ₹31 crore of in-force premium. Umeed had decomposed along the wrong axis: in a once-a-year purchase the repeat dimension that matters is survival across periods, not occurrences within one.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Three factors as three independent targets. The warning is the first quarter in which every team hits its number and the North Star misses. The question: whose plan moved a factor they do not own? Caught late, a company spends a planning cycle rewarding mix shift.

Chasing a factor near its ceiling. The warning is diminishing experimental lift — the third frequency test returning a third of the first one's effect. The question: what does the top decile already do, that being the practical ceiling? Late, it costs a year of engineering aimed at a saturated dial.

Denominator drift. The warning is a discontinuity in a factor with no counterpart in absolute counts. The question: has the base definition changed, and who approved it? Caught late, every year-on-year comparison in the board pack is wrong, and an auditor finds it first.

Confusing localisation with causation. The warning is a roadmap justified by a factor movement with no experiment attached. The question: what else changed in those weeks? The late cost is Umeed's: a budget spent moving the factor that reported the symptom.

Reporting a blended engagement score. The warning is leadership asking why engagement is up and revenue flat. The question: are depth and frequency ever shown on the same line? Caught late, a team optimises a composite no customer experiences and nobody can decompose afterwards.

Ignoring the interaction term. The warning is a recurring unexplained residual of five to ten per cent. The question: were contributions computed additively on percentages? The cost is corrosive over four quarters: the team stops trusting its own attribution and argues from anecdote.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does breadth lead or follow? The penetration-first school rests on decades of panel data across packaged goods, services and now apps, showing loyalty measures are largely predictable from penetration and that brands grow by reaching more people; on that evidence a frequency programme aimed at existing users is close to a category error. The loop school rests on a different corpus — products where usage generates the supply, content and rankings that attract the next user. For the penetration school to be wrong the loop must overcome an observed empirical regularity, which it plausibly does in marketplaces and content platforms and plausibly does not in commodity retail.

Should factors be owned separately at all? One camp argues that delegable metrics are the only reason to decompose, and that without single-threaded ownership a decomposition is an analysis, not a management system. The other argues that because every lever moves neighbouring factors, separate ownership guarantees mix-shift externalities, and the right unit of accountability is the North Star itself with the factors as diagnostics. The first points to the incoherence of teams that own nothing; the second to quarters like Unnat's. Settling it needs evidence that guardrail targets actually restrain teams, and that evidence is absent.

Aggregate identity or individual-level model? The probabilistic school holds that three population averages are a lossy summary of a heterogeneous distribution, that the covariance structure carries most of the decision-relevant information, and that fitted individual-level models predict behaviour materially better. The identity school replies that the decomposition is an organising tool rather than a forecasting one, that its exactness is its virtue in a room full of agendas, and that no executive committee was ever run on a fitted heterogeneity parameter. Both are right about different jobs.

Is a single North Star worth decomposing? A minority holds that choosing one rate forces false commensurability — that comparing a Bengali question bank with an inference-heavy explanation flow through "questions per learner" obscures that one serves access and the other depth of learning, lending spurious precision to a values judgement. The counter is that the alternative, judging incommensurable proposals by seniority and conviction, is not obviously better. This disagreement is least likely to be resolved by data.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the framework produces the three-factor chart. Someone who has internalised it argues about definitions first and arithmetic second, knowing the definitions determine the arithmetic; forecasts all three factors before a launch, including the two not being targeted, and treats a surprise in a neighbour as the most informative result; reconstructs the North Star weekly from its three reported factors as a checksum, treating a failure as urgent rather than cosmetic; and can say which factor in the product is structurally immovable — set by physics, contract, regulation or the customer's calendar — and staffs accordingly.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Bhide funded the language expansion at ₹6.4 crore and shelved the deeper explanation flow, on three grounds: breadth had the largest headroom, its cost per relative point was a quarter of depth's, and depth alone carried a recurring inference bill scaling with success. She kept the streak engine but capped its notifications, having established from the nine flat weeks that it had raised frequency 4.9 per cent while breadth fell 4.9 per cent — a trade the North Star reported as nothing at all. She also asked Nadgouda for a quality-adjusted depth series: Ushas would eventually want its tutor to make learners faster, and the current metric would call that a failure.

Sheth did the opposite of what his own arithmetic first suggested. Having seen that activating supervisor seats would deliver a third of its promised gain, he repriced three large renewals on active rather than licensed seats — shrinking his own denominator, which lifted breadth to 0.71 with no behaviour change — and put the quarter's engineering into depth, via a quality-check workflow that added confirmed lines per shift in precisely the accounts whose renewal was at risk. He told his board the breadth improvement was a definitional artefact and should not be counted as performance, which is a sentence very few product leaders say aloud.

Discussion questions. First: Bhide chose breadth on cost per relative point, but the penetration-first school would have reached the same conclusion from a different premise. Does the reasoning matter if the decision is the same, and what future decision would the two premises split on? Second: Sheth improved a metric by changing its denominator and said so. When is redefining the base legitimate measurement rather than narrative, and who holds that authority? Third: what test, applied before any budget is committed, would have told Umeed that survival across periods was the right decomposition for its category?

13. Going deeper

North Star metric — the thing being decomposed; choose it badly and all three factors inherit the error. Input vs output; leading vs lagging — the three factors are outputs too, and each needs leading indicators to be actionable in-quarter. Metric trees and driver models — the general form, these three becoming one layer with drivers beneath. Building a metrics dashboard — how factors, owners and cadences become a weekly artefact. What makes a good metric — whether your depth unit is worth optimising. Vanity vs actionable metrics — why a flattering base is the commonest vanity move. GAME framework — an alternative for teams that find the identity too narrow. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — which team can move each factor. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — why a ratio needs a stated denominator. Attention, transaction, productivity games — which factor binds in each kind of business.

Breadth × Depth × Frequency

How many, how much, how often — the three dials that decompose a North Star metric into things a team can actually move.

1. A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meher Advani, VP of Growth at Tez Mart, a quick-commerce grocery app operating in eleven Indian cities, had eleven weeks before the December festive-and-winter peak and one incremental crore of engineering capacity to spend. The board had approved a single big bet — not three small ones — and wanted it argued in numbers, not conviction. Tez Mart's North Star metric, agreed with the CEO a year earlier, was Weekly GMV per Registered User: total order value delivered each week, divided by everyone who had ever signed up in that city, whether or not they had ordered lately. In Pune, the company's largest and most mature market, that number had been flat at roughly ₹106 for six straight weeks, after two years of steady growth.

Three teams had competing proposals. Catalog wanted budget to add fifteen new categories — pharmacy, pet supplies, party goods — arguing that too many registered users never found a reason to open the app at all. Merchandising wanted to redesign the cart page to push bundles and larger baskets. Retention wanted to launch a paid membership, Tez Club, betting that people who already ordered would simply order more often if the delivery fee disappeared. Each team had a growth story. None of them, on their own, explained why the North Star had stopped moving. Meher's job that week was to find out which of the three levers — how many people ordered, how much they bought, or how often they came back — was actually the one holding Tez Mart flat, before a single rupee of the peak-season budget was committed.

2. The idea

Breadth × depth × frequency is a way of splitting a North Star metric that is really a rate — value or activity per person, per period — into three multiplied factors, each of which a team can own, instrument and move independently. Breadth asks how many of the people you could reach actually engage at all in a given period. Depth asks how much each engaged person does when they show up — order size, minutes watched, features used. Frequency asks how often an engaged person repeats the behaviour within that period. Multiply the three together, scaled by the size of the base population, and you reconstruct the North Star exactly; nothing is lost and nothing is double-counted, because each engaged person's contribution is breadth's fraction of the base, times their depth, times their frequency.

The framing has no single inventor with a named paper behind it; it crystallised inside the growth teams at large consumer internet companies in the early 2010s — Facebook's growth group under Chamath Palihapitiya is usually credited with popularising it internally around 2009–2012 — as those teams discovered that "increase engagement" was too vague a mandate to staff, and that engagement itself decomposed cleanly into how many people did a thing, how much they did, and how often. It later entered mainstream product-management teaching through growth-marketing courses such as Reforge, and now sits alongside input-versus-output and leading-versus-lagging metrics as one of the standard tools for turning a single North Star number into a small set of metrics a team can actually be held accountable for moving. The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: our North Star didn't move because breadth and depth held steady while frequency quietly slipped, so the fix has to attack frequency, not add more categories or bigger baskets.

3. How it actually works

The first step, usually skipped, is deciding what "engaged" means precisely enough to count — for Tez Mart, an engaged user in a week was anyone who completed at least one delivered order, not merely opened the app or added an item to a cart. Vague definitions of engagement are the single most common reason two people compute breadth × depth × frequency for the same business and get different numbers. The second step is choosing the time window for frequency and breadth together — a week, for a grocery habit; a month, for something bought quarterly — because frequency measured over the wrong window either saturates at a meaningless one order-per-window or dilutes real repeat behaviour into noise.

With engagement and window fixed, breadth is simply engaged users in the window divided by the registered base; depth is total value (or the chosen depth unit — items, minutes, features) divided by engaged users; frequency is total occurrences of the behaviour divided by engaged users. The three multiply back to the North Star: breadth × depth × frequency = value per registered user. The step practitioners most often leave implicit is checking that depth and frequency are not secretly measuring the same thing from two angles — if depth is "items per order" and frequency is "orders per week," they are independent; if depth were instead defined as "items per week," it would already contain frequency, and multiplying the three together would double-count activity and inflate the reconstructed North Star.

4. The arithmetic, twice

In the flat week, 18% ordered at least once (breadth = 0.18), the average order value across ordering users was ₹420 (depth), and each ordering user placed 1.4 orders that week (frequency). Multiplying the three factors gives value per registered user: 0.18 × 420 × 1.4 = ₹105.84, matching the observed North Star of roughly ₹106. Total weekly GMV in Pune was ₹105.84 × 1,00,000 ≈ ₹1.06 crore.

Meher then ran the second pass Retention had proposed: if Tez Club's reorder reminders lifted frequency from 1.4 to 1.7 orders per ordering user per week, with breadth and depth untouched, the North Star rose to 0.18 × 420 × 1.7 = ₹128.52, a 21.4% gain, worth roughly ₹22.7 lakh a week in Pune alone. Catalog's competing pitch — adding categories to lift breadth from 18% to 23%, a five-percentage-point gain that was itself optimistic for eleven weeks of work — produced ₹135.24, a slightly larger number on paper but resting on an acquisition assumption nobody could commit to hitting. The arithmetic did not settle the argument by itself; it did what breadth × depth × frequency is actually for, which was to force each team's story into a comparable, falsifiable number before the money moved.

5. What a learner must get past

The three factors are not equally elastic

Breadth usually moves slowest, because it requires either new users or dormant users re-engaging, both of which run through acquisition or lifecycle marketing cycles measured in months. Frequency is often the fastest dial in a mature product, because it can be moved by triggers, defaults and habit loops aimed at people who are already convinced. A team that treats all three as equally cheap to move will chronically over-invest in breadth campaigns that take a quarter to show results.

Depth and frequency are easy to conflate

"Engagement went up" can mean either that engaged users bought more per visit or that they visited more often, and these call for opposite fixes — a bigger cart nudges depth, a reminder nudges frequency. Reporting a single blended "engagement score" without separating the two routinely sends a team fixing the wrong surface.

The base population you divide by is a choice, not a fact

Meher's breadth was engaged users over all registered users ever, including people who signed up two years ago and never returned; a narrower base of "users active in the last 90 days" would have produced a much higher, flattering breadth figure for the same behaviour. Any comparison across teams or over time requires the same base definition, stated explicitly.

Multiplying three noisy estimates compounds their noise

Each factor carries its own measurement error and seasonal wobble; multiplying three imprecise weekly numbers together can make the reconstructed North Star swing more than any single input did, which is why most teams track the three factors on rolling averages rather than raw weekly snapshots.

The decomposition explains the past; it does not choose the future by itself

Knowing that frequency fell tells you where the shortfall came from, not whether raising frequency is the right strategic bet — a company deliberately trading frequency for higher-margin depth, say by pushing bulk orders, would see the same numbers and want the opposite response.

It says nothing about why

Breadth, depth and frequency are descriptive, not causal. A frequency drop might reflect a rival's faster delivery, a stockout in a popular category, or a pricing change — the framework tells a team where to look, never what it finds there.

Segments hide inside the average

An aggregate frequency of 1.4 can mask a loyal cohort ordering four times a week and a much larger cohort ordering once a fortnight; a thoughtful newcomer should always ask whether the number is a single population's behaviour or a blend of very different ones before proposing a company-wide fix.

6. How the picture changes by context

In a consumer product like Tez Mart, all three factors are usually visible and instrumentable within days, because behaviour is frequent and the funnel is short — which is exactly why the framework was born in consumer growth teams. In B2B software, frequency is often weekly or monthly by design, breadth can mean either how many licensed seats log in or how many accounts use the product at all, and depth is commonly redefined as the number of distinct features or workflows a customer relies on — a Freshworks-style helpdesk platform might treat "depth" as tickets resolved per agent rather than any rupee figure, since the buyer and the user are different people. In a marketplace, the decomposition has to be run twice, once for the demand side and once for supply, because a marketplace like a home-services platform can show healthy customer-side breadth and frequency while its supplier side is thin, and the blended North Star will hide exactly that imbalance.

Stage matters too: an early-stage company with a few thousand users should be suspicious of precise breadth or frequency percentages, since small samples make the three factors jumpy and easy to over-interpret from noise; the more useful early discipline is simply defining the three consistently so that later growth is measurable against a real baseline. A large, mature company like Tez Mart, with years of stable data, can instead trust small percentage-point moves in any one factor and cost them out in rupees, exactly as Meher did.

7. Where teams go wrong

Chasing breadth with a flat metric. Symptom: acquisition spend rises, signups rise, the North Star barely moves. Misunderstanding: new users add to the denominator of breadth before they add much to the numerator, so an acquisition push can mechanically depress breadth in the short run even while doing its job. Diagnostic: check breadth separately for cohorts older than ninety days; if it is healthy there, the campaign is working and the blended number is just noisy.

Reporting one merged "engagement" number. Symptom: leadership asks why engagement is up but revenue is flat. Misunderstanding: depth and frequency were blended into a single score that rose on depth while frequency quietly fell. Diagnostic: always report the three factors on one line together, never a single composite, so a rise in one cannot mask a fall in another.

Comparing periods with different base definitions. Symptom: breadth appears to jump after a "data cleanup." Misunderstanding: someone quietly redefined the registered base, often by purging dormant accounts, which mechanically raises breadth with no behaviour change at all. Diagnostic: re-run last quarter's breadth using this quarter's base definition before trusting any change.

Treating the three factors as independent when they trade off. Symptom: a frequency-boosting promotion launches and depth quietly falls. Misunderstanding: cheap, frequent small orders can cannibalise a few larger ones, leaving the North Star roughly flat while the team celebrates a frequency win. Diagnostic: watch all three factors together for at least four weeks after any lever is pulled, not just the one the campaign targeted.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Meher's decision starts, weeks before the board meeting, with a dashboard that already shows breadth, depth and frequency on one line for every city, each with a named owner, a monthly cadence, and a one-sentence statement of the decision it informs — Catalog owns breadth, Merchandising owns depth, Retention owns frequency. When Pune goes flat, the team does not debate whose instinct is right; it reads the line, sees frequency alone has slipped from 1.6 to 1.4 over six weeks while the other two held, and asks why before proposing a fix — discovering, in this telling, that a competitor's fifteen-minute delivery promise in three Pune neighbourhoods had quietly pulled repeat orders away without touching how many people tried Tez Mart at all. The proposal that reaches the board is then a frequency fix sized against a frequency problem, with the ₹22.7-lakh weekly upside shown against the cost of Tez Club's reminder engine, rather than three teams each defending their own metric.

9. What Meher decided

Meher recommended Tez Club's reorder-reminder programme over both the catalog expansion and the cart redesign, not because frequency was inherently the "right" lever but because it was the one the data implicated, the fastest to move, and the only proposal whose ₹22.7-lakh weekly gain rested on a factor that had actually changed. The board approved a six-city rollout ahead of the festive peak, with a rule attached: if frequency recovered but the North Star still lagged, breadth and depth would be re-examined before another rupee moved. The next things worth learning are how leading indicators can catch a frequency slip before it shows up in the North Star at all, and how to build the three factors into a proper metric tree with drivers underneath each one, so the next flat week takes an afternoon to diagnose rather than a full board cycle.

Two questions worth sitting with: when your own product's growth stalls, do you actually know which of the three factors moved, or only that "engagement" did? And if the answer came back "frequency," would your team have the instrumentation in place this week to find out — or would it take eleven weeks, like Tez Mart's, to even ask the right question?

Chitrapat: How Many, How Often, How Long

Hyderabad, July 2026. A regional-language streaming service has ₹96 crore, three proposals and one number it has promised the board it will double.

1. The room on the eleventh floor

At a quarter past nine on the morning of Tuesday 28 July 2026, Vidya Anantharaman walked into the eleventh-floor conference room of Chitrapat's office in Madhapur, Hyderabad, carrying a single sheet of paper. The monsoon had broken over the city the previous night and the Outer Ring Road was still flooded near Gachibowli, so two of the six people she expected were on video from home.

Vidya was vice-president of product at Chitrapat, a regional-language streaming service founded in 2019. On Friday, 31 July, the board's content and product committee would meet to lock the FY27 slate and the product roadmap together, as it did every year before the festive season. Vidya had been asked to recommend how ₹96 crore — the whole discretionary pool for content acquisition and product engineering — should be divided. Three proposals were on the table, each sponsored by a different executive, and each aimed, though nobody had put it this way yet, at a different part of the same equation.

The sheet of paper in her hand had one line on it, written the previous evening after a call with her data scientist in Toronto: 18.0 million paid viewing hours = 1.68 million viewers × 7.66 viewing days × 1.40 hours per day. Everything that followed came out of that line.

2. Chitrapat

Chitrapat streams films, series and dubbed catalogue in Telugu, Marathi, Bengali and Kannada. It was founded by Suhasini Gokhale, a former television producer, on a thesis that Indian streaming had been built for English and Hindi audiences and that a subscriber in Vijayawada or Nashik would pay for depth in her own language rather than breadth in someone else's. Seven years later the company had 2.90 million paying subscriptions and revenue of ₹412 crore in FY26, with plans at ₹99 a month and ₹499 a year and a diaspora tier at $4.99 a month.

The competitive set is crowded and getting more so. Aha, Hoichoi and Sun NXT occupy the same regional-language ground. ZEE5 and SonyLIV bundle regional content into national subscriptions. JioHotstar, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video buy the biggest Telugu and Marathi titles outright when they want them, at prices Chitrapat cannot match. Roughly 43 per cent of Chitrapat's paying base arrives through telecom bundles — prepaid and postpaid packs from Jio and Airtel — which brought volume at a fraction of the direct price and, as the company was discovering, brought it with a catch.

The engineering team sits in Bengaluru and Pune; product design is led by Ines Hartmann in Berlin, hired for her work on low-bandwidth video interfaces; the analytics function is run by Deepa Krishnan in Toronto; partner and customer success for overseas markets by Tarun Menon in Singapore; and North American diaspora distribution by Ravi Shanbhag out of Edison, New Jersey. Chitrapat's largest single overseas partner is Khaleej Sky Media in Dubai, which resells a Gulf diaspora bundle to about 140,000 households.

3. The situation

In January 2026 the board had adopted paid viewing hours per month as Chitrapat's North Star metric, on the argument that hours watched by someone who pays is the only number that both measures value delivered and predicts renewal. The target for FY27 was ambitious: from 18.0 million monthly hours to 34 million within seven quarters.

Deepa's team had spent June breaking the number into its three parts — how many subscribers actually watch in a month, how many days each of them watches, and how long they watch on a viewing day — and computing it separately for each way a subscriber had arrived. Exhibit 1 is the result, and it startled the executive team more than anything else in the quarter. Of 2.90 million paying subscriptions, only 1.68 million produced a single minute of viewing in June. The gap sat almost entirely in the telecom-bundled base, where two out of three paying subscriptions were dormant.

The three executives read Exhibit 1 in three different ways. Aparna Sethi, who runs growth and partnerships from Gurugram, saw a channel that had delivered 1.24 million paying subscriptions at ₹96 each and a second telecom deal, ready to sign, that would deliver 900,000 more. Krishna Rao, the chief content officer, saw 1.40 hours a day and said that a company whose subscribers watch less than ninety minutes when they watch at all does not have an engagement problem but a content problem, and that one genuine tentpole film would fix it. Vidya, reading the same table alongside Deepa's second analysis, saw something else: that the factor which varied most across channels was not hours per day at all — it was how many days a month people came back.

Exhibit 2 was the piece Deepa had stayed up to finish, and it complicated Krishna's argument. Whether a subscriber watched for one hour or two and a half on a viewing day had almost no bearing on whether she renewed. How many separate days she opened the app had an enormous bearing. A subscriber in the nine-to-twelve-day band renewed at more than twice the rate of one in the three-to-five-day band. If Chitrapat's real objective was a growing base of paying, watching subscribers, frequency was where the money was — but frequency is also the factor Chitrapat had invested in least, because its slate had always been built around films and eight-episode seasons released all at once.

Tarun, in Singapore, had a different complication. Khaleej Sky Media in Dubai renewed its reselling agreement in February and had asked for a Gulf diaspora bundle priced at AED 19 a month. Tarun's warning was blunt on the call: the Dubai households watched 12.4 days a month, the best frequency of any cohort Chitrapat had, and they watched almost entirely Friday to Saturday. Ravi, in New Jersey, reported the mirror image for North America — high hours per session, low days, because the diaspora watched a film on a weekend and then nothing for a fortnight.

4. The people

Vidya Anantharaman, VP Product, Hyderabad. Must make the recommendation on Friday. Wants a plan that raises the North Star in a way that survives the year, and is aware her own credibility now rests on a number she helped choose.

Aparna Sethi, Head of Growth and Partnerships, Gurugram. Carries a board-visible target for paid subscriptions, not for hours. She has a second telecom bundle negotiated and believes Chitrapat cannot afford to let a competitor take the slot.

Krishna Rao, Chief Content Officer, Hyderabad and Mumbai. Wants a ₹58-crore tentpole Telugu film for Dussehra. Argues, with some justice, that Chitrapat's brand was built by two hit films and that product mechanics cannot substitute for something people want to watch.

Deepa Krishnan, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Built Exhibits 1 and 2. Cautions that the renewal-versus-frequency relationship is observational — committed subscribers watch more often and also renew — and that the causal claim needs a test.

Ines Hartmann, Head of Design, Berlin. Supports a frequency push but has told Vidya that the obvious mechanics — daily notifications, streaks, a countdown — will not work the same way on a 4G connection in a Tier-3 town as they did in the products she designed in Europe, and that a weekly episodic rhythm is the more honest lever.

Tarun Menon, Head of International Partnerships, Singapore. Wants the Dubai bundle approved, and wants his best-frequency cohort recognised in the plan.

5. Last year's evidence

Chitrapat had run something close to Krishna's proposal before. Vaari, a ₹41-crore Marathi-and-Telugu film, launched on the Dussehra weekend of October 2025. Exhibit 3 records what happened.

The pattern in Exhibit 3 is a spike in depth, a smaller and partly temporary spike in breadth, and a fall in frequency — because subscribers spent their viewing time on one long film instead of spreading it across the week. Two months later every factor was back within a few per cent of where it had started. A tentpole, on this evidence, buys a very good October and does not change the shape of the business.

6. The options

Option A — the second telecom bundle (₹52 crore). Sign Aparna's deal. Chitrapat would gain roughly 900,000 bundled subscriptions over twelve months at ₹96 each. On the observed behaviour of bundled subscribers — a third of them view, 4.1 days, 1.15 hours — this adds about 1.24 million monthly hours, a 6.9 per cent lift on the North Star, and about 8.6 lakh of paying subscriptions to the headline count. The upside is scale, distribution and a slot a competitor cannot then take. The cost is that the renewal decision belongs to the operator, revenue per subscription is one-fifth of direct, and the blended ratios fall further, making next year's engagement numbers look worse even if nothing has deteriorated.

Option B — the weekly rhythm (₹34 crore). Rebuild the release model around frequency: a 22-minute daily serial in Telugu and Marathi commissioned at ₹14 crore for 260 episodes, weekly episodic release for all new series instead of full-season drops, a Friday "new this week" rail, WhatsApp release reminders in place of push notifications, and ₹6 crore of engineering to fix the UPI autopay mandate flow, which currently fails for 19 per cent of renewals. The upside is that it targets the factor Exhibit 2 links to renewal, and it is the cheapest of the three. The cost is that it is slow, invisible in the trade press, and untested at Chitrapat; and Krishna's objection that nobody subscribes to a service for a daily serial is not frivolous.

Option C — the tentpole (₹58 crore). Buy Krishna's Dussehra film. The upside is a spike of the kind Exhibit 3 records, real brand salience against Aha and JioHotstar in a festive quarter, and leverage in future content negotiations. The cost is ₹58 crore for a month of depth, a probable dip in frequency while it runs, and a signup mix skewed to monthly plans that lapse.

Vidya can also mix: the three proposals are not mutually exclusive, but ₹96 crore does not fund all of them, and Suhasini has said she will not approve a plan that funds all three thinly.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Write Chitrapat's North Star as breadth × frequency × depth for each channel in Exhibit 1. What does the comparison between the telecom-bundle row and the direct-annual row tell you that the blended row conceals?

2. Using Exhibit 3, decompose the change in paid viewing hours from September to October 2025 into the contribution of each factor, and then explain why the December column matters more than the October column.

3. Deepa's caution about Exhibit 2 is that the relationship is observational. Design the cheapest experiment that would tell Chitrapat whether raising viewing frequency causes renewal to rise.

4. What should Vidya recommend on Friday, how should she divide the ₹96 crore, and what would she say to Aparna about the telecom slot she is being asked to give up?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a test of whether you can resist the headline number. Chitrapat's North Star — paid viewing hours — is a reasonable choice, and every one of the three options raises it. The lens that makes the options comparable is the decomposition: paid viewing hours are the product of how many subscribers watch, how often each of them watches, and how long each viewing day lasts. Once the number is written that way, each option is revealed to be a bet on a different factor, and the factors do not behave alike.

A well-reasoned answer does four things. It computes the identity per channel rather than in aggregate, and notices that the blended frequency of 7.66 days and depth of 1.40 hours describe nobody: the bundled subscriber watches four days at barely over an hour, the direct annual subscriber more than twice as often. It reads Exhibit 3 as evidence about the durability of a depth win, not merely about its size — the October column is impressive and the December column is the verdict. It treats Exhibit 2 as strong but observational, and says what it would do to test the causal claim. And it connects each factor to the money: ₹96 crore buying hours at ₹42 per incremental monthly hour under Option A, against a far smaller and slower but compounding effect under Option B.

One defensible path: fund Option B in full at ₹34 crore, commission a four-part limited series rather than the tentpole at about ₹40 crore, hold ₹22 crore back, and decline the telecom bundle in its current form while asking Aparna to renegotiate it as a revenue-share with an activation floor — the operator is paid only on subscriptions that view at least three days a month. The reasoning is that frequency is the only factor which both moves the North Star and predicts renewal, that it is the cheapest factor to move and the furthest from its natural ceiling for a service whose subscribers watch a quarter of the days in a month, and that breadth bought at ₹96 a subscription with a two-thirds dormancy rate is not growth but the appearance of growth — it raises the North Star by 6.9 per cent while pushing the blended ratios down and handing the renewal decision to Jio's product team. The limited series is the concession to Krishna, and it is a real one: a four-part weekly release is a depth asset released on a frequency schedule, which is the nearest thing to a plan that both executives can sign. What Vidya must not do is accept all three at reduced scale, because a thin tentpole is the one version of a tentpole that reliably fails.

Finally, note what the decomposition does not settle. It cannot tell Vidya whether a daily Telugu serial will be any good, and a bad one will move no factor at all. Arithmetic narrows the argument to the right question; it does not answer it.
